Arrant means complete, total, and absolute — but here's the critical catch: it is only ever used with bad or negative things. It's a word that takes something already negative and cranks it up to the maximum possible degree. Think of it as a supercharger for negative qualities.

When you call something arrant, you are saying: "This is not just bad. This is the worst, most extreme, most thorough version of this bad thing that you can imagine. There is nothing left out. It is 100% this."
The Key Feature That Makes It Special

In English, words like complete, total, utter, sheer, downright can also mean "absolute" — but they can go with both positive and negative things. You can say "a complete success" or "a complete failure." You can say "utter joy" or "utter chaos."

Arrant cannot do this. You will never hear "arrant brilliance" or "arrant kindness." The word is exclusively devoted to negativity — to faults, flaws, vices, and bad qualities. This is what makes it sharp and distinctive. When you see it, you instantly know that what follows is something negative, taken to its absolute extreme.

Let's go through several real uses, and for each one, break down exactly what the word is doing:

"That is arrant nonsense."

This doesn't just mean the idea is wrong or silly. It means the idea is completely, thoroughly, and totally without sense — not even a grain of truth, logic, or merit survives. The speaker is wiping it out entirely.

"He is an arrant coward."

This is not saying the person is somewhat cowardly or often cowardly. It's saying cowardice defines this person to the fullest possible degree. There is no bravery hiding anywhere. He is a coward through and through, completely and without exception.

"She told arrant lies."

These weren't half-truths or exaggerations. These were lies in the purest, most complete sense — deliberate, total, shameless falsehoods.

"The plan was arrant folly."

The plan wasn't just unwise or risky. It was thoroughly, absolutely, and completely foolish — folly of the highest order, with no trace of wisdom or good judgment to be found anywhere in it.

"He is an arrant knave."

A knave is a dishonest, unscrupulous person. Calling someone an arrant knave says he is not merely somewhat dishonest — he is a knave in the fullest, most complete sense of the word.

Arrant is not a neutral, dry word. It carries a tone of strong judgment, contempt, or exasperation. When someone uses it, they are not calmly describing something — they are expressing that something is outrageously bad, to a degree that deserves emphasis and strong condemnation.

It has a slightly formal, literary feel to it. You're more likely to encounter it in writing — in novels, essays, journalism, speeches — than in everyday casual conversation. But when a person does use it in speech, it sounds deliberate and forceful, like someone who means exactly what they're saying and wants you to feel the full weight of it.
What Kinds of Words Pair With It

Arrant almost always sits in front of nouns referring to:

  • Negative personal qualities: fool, coward, liar, hypocrite, villain, scoundrel, knave
  • Bad ideas or statements: nonsense, folly, rubbish, absurdity
  • Dishonest or immoral behavior: theft, fraud, deception

It will never sit in front of positive nouns. If you ever feel tempted to write "arrant genius" or "arrant beauty" — stop. That's not how the word works.
A Simple Test to Know When to Use It

Ask yourself three questions before using arrant:

  1. Is the thing I'm describing negative? ✅ Required.
  2. Is it total and without exception — not just partial or occasional? ✅ Required.
  3. Am I making a strong judgment about it — not just neutrally noting it? ✅ Required.

If all three answers are yes, arrant is likely the right word.
Summing It Up in One Sentence

Arrant means complete and absolute — but reserved exclusively for negative qualities, always implying that the thing in question is thoroughly and without exception bad, to the fullest possible degree.
